concept: one_line: The player in last place sets the height of the bar by clicks nobody else can read, and everyone then commits, in secret and simultaneously, to the tallest piece from their own stock they believe will still fit under it. | slug: clearance | arm: measurement-dexterity | emotion: nerve, then loud schadenfreude when the leader's piece kisses the bar | piggyback: simultaneous commit and reveal, highest takes the round (a trick, without cards) | audience: adults who like push-your-luck round games — Perudo, Camel Up, Skull — and want the luck replaced with an estimate they own; 14+ | players 2-4, light, target_minutes 25 | fun_correct_bet: the entire decision is 'how tall is that gap, really, and how tall is my third-best piece, really' — and both quantities are physical facts about parts on the table, not numbers. The bar-setter's skill is picking a gap where their own stock has a clean answer and everyone else's stock has a coin flip. Ignore the print and you are guessing every round. | nearest_known: Perudo and Skull (simultaneous commit, escalating bid); Cabo-style closest-without-busting scoring; limbo as a party stunt. I know of no published game where the bid is a physical height and the bust is a piece touching a bar.
mechanism: A printed gantry with a threaded column: the crossbar rises 0.5 mm per detented click, and only the setter's side carries an unmarked scale, so the table knows the number of clicks and nothing else. 30 printed pieces, six per player, heights randomised across a 0.4 mm ladder from 18 to 30 mm, held open in front of each player — your stock is public, its exact heights are not. Each round: last place sets the bar, everyone hides one piece in a fist behind their printed screen, reveal together, then slide in turn order in one pass, no lifting, no rocking. Tallest piece that clears takes the round. A piece that touches the bar is out of the game permanently, and if two pieces tie for tallest, both are lost and nobody scores. Play until one stock is empty.
physical_hook: Cardboard breaks: the bid is a solid object passing through a real gap, and the bust condition is contact. Flatten it and you are comparing two printed integers, which is arithmetic with a screen printed on it. Molding breaks: a mould gives every copy the same 30 heights, and the day one group writes the list down the estimate is gone and the game is arithmetic again; printing generates a fresh random ladder per copy, and the 0.5 mm detent screw is a tuned mechanism you iterate at quantity one rather than cut into steel.
title: Clearance
